chapter.title: Toys, Games and Sports Equipment; Parts and Accessories Thereof

page.h1: HTS Chapter 95: Toys, Games and Sports Equipment; Parts and Accessories Thereof — U.S. Exports & Foreign Tariffs

seo.title: U.S. Toy, Video Game & Sports Equipment Exports: Buyers & Tariffs
seo.shortDescription: The U.S. exported $6.71B of video game consoles, toys, cards and sports gear in 2025; Canada (39%) and Mexico (14%) buy most. Who buys what, and the tariffs.

intro:
The U.S. exported **$6.71 billion** of video game consoles, toys, cards, sports and exercise equipment, fishing tackle and amusement rides (HTS Chapter 95) in 2025, down **3.5%** from 2024. Games are the largest group (heading 9504, **$2.99 billion**, 45%), led by **video game consoles** and their controllers and parts (9504.50, **$1.28 billion**, down 14.9%), coin-operated games (**$605 million**) and playing and trading cards (**$540 million**, up 46.8%). Sports equipment follows (9506, **$2.02 billion**), led by exercise machines (9506.91, **$710 million**) and golf clubs, balls and other golf gear (**$690 million**), then toys, dolls and puzzles (9503, **$1.17 billion**). **Canada** buys **38.7%** and **Mexico** **13.7%**; the UK, Australia and Japan take 3.7–4.5% each.

Most buyers charge little or nothing: qualifying U.S. goods enter Canada, Mexico, Australia and South Korea free under their trade agreements, the EU has charged **0%** on every U.S. Chapter 95 line since **July 1, 2026**, and Japan and the UK charge 0–4%. The exception is **Canada**: since **September 8, 2026** it charges a **50%** surtax on U.S. video game consoles, exercise equipment, other sports and outdoor-game gear, golf equipment other than complete clubs and balls, and fishing rods, with no CUSMA exemption. **China** adds **10%** to every U.S. good, and Brazil's normal rates (20%, 35% on most toys) are the highest among the large buyers. For toys, what decides access is mostly product safety: toy-safety rules and marks such as the EU's CE marking, the UK's UKCA, Brazil's INMETRO certificate and China's CCC.

keyTakeaways: Canada, which buys 38.7% of U.S. Chapter 95 exports, charges 50% on U.S. video game consoles, exercise machines, other sports gear, golf parts and fishing rods since September 8, 2026. Toys, playing and trading cards, complete golf clubs, golf balls and Christmas articles are not on its list and still enter free under CUSMA.

U.S. sales to Mexico, the second buyer, fell 23.9% in 2025 to $922 million and another 25.9% in January–August 2026, while Canada held roughly flat (+1.0% in 2025, −4.4% so far in 2026) and Australia grew 26.6%.

Playing and trading cards (9504.40) were the fastest-growing large line in 2025, up 46.8% to $540 million; the EU, the third-largest market after Canada and Mexico, has let them and every other U.S. Chapter 95 good in at 0% since July 1, 2026.

China adds 10% to U.S. toys and consoles on top of a 0% normal rate (6% on most sports gear), and two dates could raise that: December 31, 2026 (tariff exclusions end) and January 10, 2027 (24-point suspension ends).
